instructions:
You judge whether muted viewers understood short scenes of animated book-summary videos. This file holds several items, each from a DIFFERENT scene; each has the narration spoken over the scene, the frozen answer key (what a muted viewer should understand, its cause, its effect, key facts, plausible wrong inferences, whether the narration states any causality at all, what the narrator asserts, and what the narration mentions but does NOT assert — notAsserted), and what a viewer with the sound off wrote (description). Some viewers saw three moments of the scene, some saw more moments; judge only what the description says. Judge each item on its own.
1. cause — CORRECT (the viewer's cause matches the key's cause in meaning), WRONG (contradicts it), NOT_SHOWN (unclear / missing / something else). effect — the same against the key's effect. If the key says supportsCausality: false, answer "NA" for both.
2. message — MATCH (the viewer's message states the key's understanding), PARTIAL (its subject or half of it), MISS.
3b. polarityError — YES if the viewer states as true (or as the narrator's point) something the key lists under notAsserted (a rejected premise, counterfactual, hypothesis, question, quoted speech, uncertain claim or the setup half of a contrast); otherwise NO.
3. wrongInference — YES if the viewer states something the key lists as a wrong inference, or a cause / claim that contradicts the narration; otherwise NO.
4. whatChanged — CORRECT if who or what the viewer says changed matches the key's effect (the thing that ends up different), WRONG if the viewer names a different change that contradicts the key, NOT_SHOWN if the viewer names no change or an unrelated one, NA if the key states no causality.
5. finalConsequence — YES if the viewer states the key's final consequence (the end state / result the narration gives), NO if not, NA if the key states no causality.
Judge meaning, not wording; be strict and literal; do not reward a description for being longer, prettier or busier.
Write ONLY a JSON array (one object per item, same order) to the output path you were given: [{"img":"…","cause":"…","effect":"…","message":"…","wrongInference":"YES|NO","polarityError":"YES|NO","whatChanged":"…","finalConsequence":"…","why":"…"}, …]

items.narration: It simply laid out the rule, begging people not to steal the wood. But crucially, it made no mention of how often the theft occurred. It provided no social proo

answerKey.understanding: A sign that simply stated a rule against stealing wood failed because it included no social proof about how common the theft was.
answerKey.cause: The sign used an injunctive norm (stating the rule) but made no mention of theft frequency
answerKey.effect: It provided no social proof, leaving a key persuasion mechanism unused
keyFacts: The sign used an injunctive norm
It told people not to steal the wood
It made no mention of how often theft occurred
It provided no social proof
wrongInferences: The sign included statistics about theft frequency
The sign's lack of social proof reduced theft rates
Cialdini's team wrote the sign to test social proof's presence
answerKey.asserted: The injunctive-norm sign stated the rule but crucially omitted any reference to how often theft occurred, thus providing no social proof.

notAsserted.why: No outcome of this sign's effectiveness is stated in this narration

notAsserted.text: Social proof was present but ignored
notAsserted.why: The narration says social proof was absent, not ignored

sees: frame 1: A light grey background suggesting an indoor scene (faint outlines of a table and chairs). A large white speech-bubble/caption box in the centre reads: 'it made no mention of how often the theft occurred'.
frame 2: Identical composition to frame 1 — same background, same caption box with the same text. No visible change.
frame 3: Identical composition again — same background, same caption box with the same text. No visible change.
description.message: A piece of information (a warning or sign) omitted the frequency of theft, which is presented as a meaningful detail.
description.wouldConfuse: All three frames look identical; without audio or surrounding context it is impossible to tell what scene is being described or what 'it' refers to — the viewer has no visual anchor for 'theft'.

answerKey.cause: Pitting academic theories against actual commercial campaigns and field trials
answerKey.effect: Readers are forced to see theory in the wild, making it a masterclass in structural analysis
keyFacts: The book bridges academic theory and commercial advertising
It is described as a masterclass in structural analysis
It forces us to see theory applied in real contexts
wrongInferences: The billboard industry inspired the academic theories
Structural analysis is taught separately from advertising examples
The book is primarily a critique of ivory-tower thinking
answerKey.asserted: The book bridges the ivory tower and the billboard by forcing us to see theory in the wild.

notAsserted.text: The theories are proven correct by the campaigns
notAsserted.why: The narration says we see theory in the wild, not that the theory is validated

notAsserted.text: The book is easy to read

sees: frame 1: Three icons are displayed in a row against a light background with faint city-skyline silhouettes: a grey open book labelled 'ANALYSIS', a dark navy compass/diamond circle icon labelled 'THEORY', and a dark cone/obelisk shape labelled 'WILD'. They are evenly spaced, all roughly the same visual weight, with no connections between them.

frame 2: The book icon ('ANALYSIS') has enlarged and turned red/pink, surrounded by a pink circle, and is now highlighted as the focal element. A dashed arrow curves from the book icon rightward, and dashed-line boxes appear over the 'THEORY' and 'WILD' labels, suggesting a flow or relationship. The compass icon has moved slightly right and closer to the cone.

frame 3: Very similar to frame 2 — the book icon remains large, red, and circled. The dashed arrow and dashed boxes are still present. The compass icon (THEORY) and cone (WILD) have moved further right, with the compass icon now appearing even further to the right of the cone, as if re-ordered or shifted.
description.changed: From frame 1 to frame 3: the ANALYSIS book icon becomes the dominant highlighted element (enlarged, red, circled), dashed arrows and boxes connect it to the other two icons, and the THEORY and WILD icons shift positions.
description.cause: An animation is showing how 'ANALYSIS' leads to or connects with 'THEORY' and 'WILD', structuring the book's content framework.
description.effect: The viewer understands that the book is organised around three categories — Analysis, Theory, Wild — with Analysis as the starting or primary element.
description.message: The narrator is explaining the structure of the book or the insight series: each insight will cover analysis, theory, and a wild/unexpected angle.
description.wouldConfuse: The re-ordering of THEORY and WILD icons between frames 2 and 3 (the compass moves to the far right, past the cone) may suggest WILD comes before THEORY, contradicting the original left-to-right order. The dashed boxes over THEORY and WILD could look like they are being crossed out or de-emphasised rather than connected.

items.narration: Nobody ever got fired for buying IBM because it's the default safe choice. Precisely. It is infinitely safer for a middle manager's career to fail conventionall

answerKey.understanding: Choosing the conventional, safe option (like IBM) protects a manager's career even if it fails, because failure by conformity is easier to justify than failure by innovation.
answerKey.cause: IBM is the default safe choice; failing conventionally is safer for a middle manager's career
answerKey.effect: It is infinitely safer to fail conventionally than unconventionally
keyFacts: IBM is cited as the default safe corporate choice
Failing conventionally is safer for a middle manager's career
The saying 'Nobody ever got fired for buying IBM' is a famous corporate adage
wrongInferences: IBM became dominant because its products were superior
Middle managers who buy IBM are more likely to be promoted
Unconventional choices are safer for a manager's career than conventional ones
answerKey.asserted: Nobody ever got fired for buying IBM because conforming to the default is the safest career move for a middle manager.

notAsserted.why: The narration makes a career-safety argument, not a product-quality claim
The narration contrasts safety levels, not universal outcomes

sees: frame 1: A cartoon man in a dark suit stands on the left in a room with a grey radial-burst background. To his right is a large orange rectangle displaying the text 'THE DEFAULT SAFE CHOICE' in white bold letters. The man's eyes are open and he looks neutral.
frame 2: The same scene. The man's eyes are now closed or nearly closed, and his mouth is slightly open — he appears to be speaking or expressing something. The orange sign is unchanged.
frame 3: The same scene again. The man's eyes are open once more and his expression has returned to neutral. The orange sign remains. No other changes.
description.changed: The character's eyes closed briefly (frame 2) and then reopened (frame 3); his mouth was slightly open in frame 2.
description.cause: The character is mid-speech — a talking/blinking animation cycle playing while the sign is on screen.
description.effect: The scene conveys that the presenter is actively talking about 'The Default Safe Choice' while the concept label stays visible.
description.message: People tend to pick the default, safe option rather than taking a risk.
description.wouldConfuse: With sound off, the blinking/talking animation is the only cue that the character is speaking; without audio, the scene change feels very minor and the viewer may not register anything is being explained.

items.narration: It's exactly why casinos force you to convert your cash into brightly colored plastic chips before you sit at the blackjack table. They need to abstract the los

answerKey.understanding: Casinos convert cash into chips to psychologically distance gamblers from real money, reducing the pain of loss and encouraging more spending.
answerKey.cause: Casinos force players to convert cash into brightly colored plastic chips
answerKey.effect: The loss is abstracted, the brain stops registering spending as giving up a real resource, friction disappears, and spending increases
keyFacts: Casinos require cash to be converted into brightly colored plastic chips
Chips abstract the loss away from real money
The brain stops treating chips as a finite survival resource
Removing friction increases spending
wrongInferences: Casinos use chips primarily for security and fraud prevention
Players spend less when using chips than cash
The chip system increases the brain's awareness of real financial loss
answerKey.asserted: Casinos use chips to abstract the loss so the brain treats money like Monopoly money, removing friction and enabling freer spending.

notAsserted.why: No fairness claim is made; the motivation given is psychological abstraction of loss

notAsserted.text: Players are unaware of chip conversion
notAsserted.why: The narration says casinos force conversion, implying players experience it

sees: frame 1: A light-coloured room background with three icons arranged horizontally: a crowd of small human figures labelled 'CASINOS', a large grey coin with a dollar sign labelled 'CASH', and a chess-knight piece labelled 'CHIPS'. All three elements are static and evenly spaced.

frame 2: The same three icons, but the coin (CASH) has moved right and now sits next to the CHIPS icon. A dashed rectangle outlines both CASH and CHIPS together, grouping them. A curved arrow drawn with a red circle at its tail points from CASINOS up and over to the CHIPS/CASH group, suggesting a directional relationship.

frame 3: The layout is identical to frame 2 — CASINOS on the left, CASH and CHIPS grouped inside a dashed rectangle on the right — with the same curved arrow. The positions appear fully settled; there is no further motion visible.
description.changed: The CASH coin moved from between CASINOS and CHIPS to beside CHIPS; a dashed grouping box appeared around CASH and CHIPS; a curved arrow appeared pointing from CASINOS to that group.
description.cause: An animation is illustrating that casinos redirect or convert cash into chips — the arrow and grouping box show that cash and chips belong together as a destination of casino action.
description.effect: The viewer understands that casinos take cash and exchange it for chips, bundling the two concepts together as the outcome of the casino relationship.
description.message: Casinos convert your cash into chips, abstracting money into a less emotionally real form.
